slides.notes: PathSignal is a prototype for spoken obstacle awareness, intended to supplement existing mobility tools. This presentation covers the problem, aim, requirements, design and selected technology. Photograph: original user-supplied development recording; it is not evidence of independent walking performance.

A small object or change in level can matter to a traveller who cannot rely on visual inspection. The project explores an extra spoken cue; it does not establish prevention of trips or injuries. Current camera testing is stationary and uses supported classes. Local need has not been quantified through a representative user study. WHO discusses functional and mobility impacts of vision impairment.

Prototype question

No local accident survey or blind-user usability study has been completed for PathSignal.

slides.notes: This aim is aligned with the original Ground Obstacle Alert Prototype problem. Earlier warning is an assessment goal, not a demonstrated outcome. The current contribution is software integration and interaction: pretrained detectors, preprocessing, image-space filtering, encounter handling, spoken alerts and observable test records. Distance and independent travel remain outside the validated scope.
text: To develop and assess a phone-based prototype that gives spoken warnings about supported objects and stair regions in a camera image.
Make local camera inference usable through accessible controls and brief audio alerts.
Measure detections, misses, unwanted alerts and warning delay under defined conditions.

slides.notes: Implementation sources: phone/App.tsx, phone/useObjectWorker.tsx, phone/worker/detector.ts, presentation-site/src/useMonitor.ts and useDetector.ts. Both apps scan snapshots and offer separate modes. Repeated scans re-arm a class after two scans without it. Browser logging includes timestamps, source, model, duration and whether speech was requested, with CSV/JSON export. The phone currently shows session counters; do not imply it has the same export log. Camera/model failure states request a pause announcement. Desktop tests do not establish all physical iPhone behaviors.

Security scope: application code does not upload camera pixels; normal hosting requests still reach Vercel, and browser font stylesheets may load externally. HTTPS protects browser delivery and enables camera access; an initial model/runtime download is required and offline browser use is not guaranteed. Usability controls and selected/disabled semantics exist, but a formal VoiceOver/user study remains pending. No acceptable end-to-end warning-latency threshold has been agreed, so this slide does not claim one. Reliability refers to implemented handling and desktop checks, not a measured real-world hazard recall rate.
text: Process images locally; request camera permission; keep API keys out of the shipped app.
Label controls for screen readers; use clear states, large controls and short alerts.
Keep inference off the main UI; measure scan duration and physical alert delay.
Handle failures explicitly; suppress repeat alerts; prevent stale scan results.
Desktop checks pass; field testing pending

slides.notes: Architecture is a simplified logical view of the current shipped applications. The selected model alone loads for a mode. YOLOX-S retains 25 COCO object labels; the separate YOLOv8n model has one stairs class. The browser uses a Web Worker; Expo uses a hidden react-native-webview processing view. Local preprocessing/decoding, filtering and encounter logic precede audio. Browser localStorage holds up to 200 scan records and exports on request; Expo currently shows counters. Hosting delivers static assets, not a server-side camera-inference API. Diagram objects and connectors are editable.

slides.notes: These are intended use cases, not evidence of completed blind-user trials. The current supervised/stationary demonstration can be run by a sighted operator. The primary actor selects a mode, controls capture and receives/repeats audio. The evaluator reviews browser scan evidence and exports it. Plain UML associations do not represent data flow. Runtime permission and availability checks are internal to the capture/scan use cases. The system boundary and use cases remain native editable slide objects.
text: Log export is available in the browser application.

slides.notes:
Current code uses Expo SDK 58, expo-camera, expo-image-manipulator and expo-audio. The browser uses getUserMedia, canvas and Web Speech; this does not imply that every browser offers identical speech behavior. Expo Go avoids a paid custom iOS build for the supported camera/WASM prototype; native LiDAR is a different signed-build path and is not active in Expo Go. TypeScript checks, local builds, browser automation and Git history support reproducibility. Vercel hosts static assets and does not process camera images in a backend.

The student/project did not train these neural networks. YOLOX-S is a publisher COCO checkpoint; only selected labels are enabled. The Roboflow artifact obstacle-detection-n3eec/1 contains one stairs class despite the broader project overview. No Kaggle fine-tuning or LLM is part of the current app. Kaggle and Roboflow supported dataset/model research; the current stair weights came from Roboflow. Roboflow keys were used only by a local access/download tool and are absent from shipped apps. The downloaded stair artifact identifies Ultralytics 8.2.0 and AGPL-3.0; the project publishes application source and licence notices.

slides.notes: The prototype supplements existing mobility tools. Silence gives no information about path clearance. Independent walking is not validated. An iPhone 15 Pro LiDAR scanner exists on the user device, but the current Expo Go/browser application does not expose a validated LiDAR distance feature. Future assessment must use fresh scenes, define conditions and thresholds, measure audible delay and failures, and keep development clips out of held-out results. These are next steps, not completed outcomes. Demo: https://pathsignal-six.vercel.app
